source_read: PDF, Schizophrenia Research 267: 182–190 (all nine pages): text; Table 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; Figs. 1 and 2 read at 300 dpi; both pools recomputed (Hedges' g, DerSimonian–Laird) from Table 1 with and without reading the Dawe and Hajebi dispersions as standard errors, the forest-plot values re-pooled, leave-one-out repeated (random and common effect), interval widths compared with group sizes; supplementary tables and figures not available.

key_findings.note: Table 1 group sizes sum to 624 and 527.
Re-pooling the twelve Fig. 2 values reproduces −0.35 (−0.54; −0.16), I² 54%, tau² 0.056.

Recomputed: omitting Mikami from the Fig. 2 values gives −0.28 (−0.44; −0.12), I² 30% with random effects, as the card says, and −0.25 (−0.38; −0.13) with a common-effect model, which matches the printed −0.254 (−0.37 to −0.13). The printed estimate therefore looks like a common-effect leave-one-out, although 2.7 states random effects for every analysis; the printed I² of 58% matches omitting most other single studies (for example Zhang, 58.0%), not Mikami. The note could say so instead of 'the method is not described'.
Fig. 1 at 300 dpi; re-pooling its own values gives −0.01 (−0.13; 0.11), I² 0%, so the pooling is consistent with the plotted inputs.

Recomputed exactly, under the stated reading of the Dawe and Hajebi dispersions as standard errors: positive −0.29 (−0.67; 0.10), tau² 0.40, I² 89%, studies from −1.93 (Mikami) and −1.11 (Alexander) to 0.54 (Srisurapanont); negative −0.44 (−0.72; −0.16), I² 79%. Eleven of the twelve Fig. 2 point estimates are reproduced (Alexander's 0.17 only with 39 vs 39 people; Mikami −2.11 against −1.05). Taking every dispersion as an SD, as printed: positive −0.35 (−0.90; 0.20), I² 94%, studies −1.98 to 1.20; negative −0.99 (−1.66; −0.33), I² 96%.
The 3.3.2 5th paragraph starts on p. 184 and ends on p. 186.

reporting_issues.note: Numbers right, assumption missing: the values 'implied' by Table 1 (−1.93 to 0.54; −0.29, −0.67 to 0.10, I² 89%) hold only when the Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 dispersions are read as standard errors (reporting issue 2). Suggested addition: 'reading those two studies' dispersions as standard errors; taking them as printed, study values −1.98 to 1.20 and −0.35 (−0.90 to 0.20), I² 94%'. Either way none of the Fig. 1 values is reproduced, and the Fig. 1 values themselves pool to the reported −0.01, so the fault lies in the study-level inputs.
With Table 1's Mikami value the pool is −0.44 (−0.72; −0.16) with Table 1 group sizes and −0.43 (−0.72; −0.15) with the Fig. 2 sizes.
Hajebi as standard errors gives −0.68 (−1.06; −0.29), identical to Fig. 2; Dawe −0.41 (−0.81; −0.01) against −0.41 (−0.82; −0.01).
Equal group sizes implied by the Fig. 2 interval widths: 38.9 (Alexander), 20.4 (Hides), 28.4 (Howells); the other nine widths fit Table 1 within rounding.
From the printed intervals: z about 0.16 (p about 0.87) and 3.6 (p about 0.0003).
35 of 53 is 66.0% and 36 of 53 is 67.9%; Dawe's reference title (p. 189) names inpatients.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is right and critically low follows from two critical items not met (7 and 11). Item 7 rests partly on a supplementary flow chart that was not available: a flow chart normally gives counts, so 'no' is the likely value, but if Supplementary Fig. 1 listed the excluded studies with reasons, item 11 alone would make the overall low confidence. The overall could be marked provisional on that item (METHODS §5.3).

risk_of_bias_domains.note: English-language, human and age limits are not justified (2.3), and AMSTAR 2's 'partial yes' requires justified restrictions. Overall unchanged.
The items listed as extracted (2.5) do not include the symptom scores.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed: similarity of positive symptoms is concluded from a result that cannot be reproduced from the review's own table, the p values are the heterogeneity tests, and 'stable outpatients' does not describe five of the twelve studies.

missed: The most heavily weighted study (Srisurapanont 2011: 30.4% of the positive pool, 13.9% of the negative) drew its two groups from two different studies, the WHO multi-site project for methamphetamine psychosis and a Thai trial of long-acting injectable risperidone for schizophrenia (Table 1, p. 186). It is a between-study comparison of groups recruited for different purposes, not a direct comparison; the card's timeline describes it as a WHO multisite comparison.

The 'PANSS' score ranges in the text do not match Table 1 (3.3.1 and 3.3.2, p. 184): positive 14.5–19.8 (methamphetamine psychosis) and 14–19.8 (schizophrenia), negative 7–17 and 8.9–19.8, include Dawe's BPRS values (19.84, 7.12, 8.98) and leave out Hajebi (31.9 and 33.4) and Howells (8 and 12); 3.3.1 also says the positive-symptom data came from 12 studies using PANSS positive scores, while 3.2 says 6 used the PANSS, 5 the BPRS and 1 the Manchester scale. Another sign that values were transcribed without checking.

Hajebi 2018's baseline PANSS positive means (31.9 and 33.4, Table 1) are those of acutely ill people, consistent with a first-episode cohort assessed at admission (reference title, p. 189), not with stable outpatients (editors' inference).
